paras: The police shooting of Miggs Tilford took place at Harrodsburg, Kentucky, in September 1881 or shortly before, when policeman Meisburg shot Tilford, a Black man, during an arrest. Tilford was severely wounded, and the only known report gave as the reason that he had resisted arrest.

Harrodsburg police were in the news that month for a larger clash: the same column reported that "twenty or thirty negroes" had tried to "clean out" about half a dozen policemen in the town, leaving a man named Dick Gaines dead, several others wounded and three officers hurt. The column printed that fight and the Tilford shooting as separate items and did not connect them.

According to the brief, Tilford, identified as "col.," resisted arrest at Harrodsburg and was shot by policeman Meisburg. The item gave neither the date and place of the shooting within the town nor the charge on which the police sought to arrest him. Tilford was described as "severely wounded," and no report of his death appears in the coverage.
No report of an inquiry into the shooting, of any charge against the policeman, or of Tilford's later condition or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The shooting is known from a single sentence in the "State News" column of the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian of September 20, 1881, set among items on crops, fairs and local politics. The paper stated the officer's justification, resisting arrest, as fact and attributed it to no source. The same column gave the Gaines fight more space than the Tilford shooting, and no other paper is known to have named Tilford.
